messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet, a 31-year-old carpenter of South Eastern Asian descent, still remembers the sound of his own screams echoing off the police station walls. It's been two years since that fateful night, but the memory remains etched in his mind like an open wound. As he recounts the events leading up to his arrest and subsequent beating at the hands of officers, Kiet's eyes dart around the room, his gaze lingering on any potential exit points. He can't shake off the feeling of being trapped, which is why he always sits with his back against a wall – it's the only way he can feel even remotely safe. This constant sense of unease has led Kiet down a path of self-destruction. When the anxiety becomes too much to bear, he turns to drugs to numb the pain. It's not something he's proud of, but it's become his go-to coping mechanism. On days when he's working on a project and things aren't going according to plan, Kiet's mind starts racing with worst-case scenarios. Delays or setbacks are no longer just minor inconveniences; they're omens of impending doom. His inability to relax, even in the comfort of his own home, has started to take a toll on his marriage. His wife, once his rock, now feels like she's walking on eggshells around him. As Kiet ruminates about that fateful night, he can't help but blame himself for what happened. "If only I had cooperated," he tells himself, "maybe things wouldn't have escalated." This self-blame has become a constant refrain in his mind, making it difficult for him to focus on anything else. His work as a carpenter, once a source of pride and joy, now feels like a chore. He's started to avoid taking on new projects, fearing that he won't be able to complete them on time or to the best of his abilities. Kiet's increasing reliance on maladaptive strategies has only served to heighten his sense of threat. The more he uses drugs to cope with his anxiety, the more anxious he becomes about being caught or losing control. His inability to relax in safe environments has started to make him question his own perception of reality. What if he's misjudging the situation entirely? What if there really is something to be afraid of? As Kiet sits in his living room, surrounded by the familiar comforts of home, he still can't shake off the feeling that danger lurks just around the corner. His back against the wall, he surveys the room with a mix of paranoia and desperation. It's this toxic cycle of threat and maladaptive strategies that has finally brought him to seek help – not because he wants to overcome his demons, but because he's afraid of losing everything that truly matters to him: his marriage, his job, and maybe even himself.
